blocks.x: Okay, it's going. Can you give us your name?
My name is Buddy Burns. I guess, well, I'm how old?
Yes, how old are you?
How old I am. I was born in 1900, 28th day of August.
What was your real name?
Nelson Buddy Burns.
Can you tell me about the first music you ever heard? Were your parents musical? Did they play anything?
Yeah, no, no one played but me. No one played but me. I was the only one that was a musician.
What was the first instrument you ever took up?
Piano.
Piano. Did you have a piano at home or have to practice on the neighborhood?
No, I had it home.
How did you come right here? You had a fidget, huh? What was some of the first music you ever heard? The first bands or where did you hear music?
Oh, I got to go back to the way. Dixieland, I heard the first was played by the Olympic band, I think. And that was...
Do you remember who was in the band?
Yeah, they had... Yeah, they had... Lib Newton... And...
A deep play? Let me stop. Oh.
No, that wasn't the right name, but...
The Olympic... It wasn't the Olympic band.
It wasn't the Olympic band. Who was in it though? They had Lib Newton...
A deep play?
He played bass fiddle. He's the one who started me on bass. It was 19... 12... 1910. And...
Who else was in the band?

Uh... The Lib was on bass and Nene was on drum. And... Tick Chambers was uh... Playing trumpet. And uh... Yank was playing trombone. And uh... Oh... Emmet was playing guitar. And... Let's see... Uh... Who else? Oh... Freddie... Freddie Kepard... Playing... Playing uh... Cornet or... Cornet or...
Cornet or...
Cornet I think it was. Cornet. One of those old time deals. And uh... Let's see who else we had there. I call uh... Carl Yank... Yeah.
Yeah.
That's about all.
Clarinet.
Who was the Clarinet? Clarinet. Yes. They had, they had Ishmann Turo was playing uh... Clarinet. No alto valve, I mean that's...
Alto horn. Alto horn, yeah. That was a dance band or was it?
Yeah, dance band. Yeah.
Did you hear any earlier music around your house when you were young, anybody singing, or did you hear any music at churches?
They, I come to start to play, they used to rehearse at my house once a week.
Well that band did.

That band. That band. Rehearse at my house once every week. Lib Newton was my sister's boyfriend. Oh yeah. My oldest sister's boyfriend. And he's the one started me on bass. Uh huh. Around 1910. Yeah.
Hmm. Did you hear any music in the churches when you were young?
Yes, I heard music in churches, I did. Uh huh.
Which church, did you belong to any church then or?
Well at that time I was uh, I was uh, a Methodist. Uh huh. But uh, after I got married, I married Catholic. And I, and I made my communion and I married Catholic.
Your wife is from downtown, I believe she said she lived across the street from some musician. Who was that?
Well we moved downtown later, as soon as we got married we moved. Well what part of town did you come from? Well we come from around uh, uh, uh, let's see uh, Seven and Howard. Seven and Howard.
Yeah.
Mm hmm. Seven and Howard.
Um, can you remember any of the other early bass players that you uh, liked?

Yeah, I liked it uh, I like, I can't call this fella Ellick, his name is Ellick. He's a very good bass player. His last name, I always wished to play bass like him when I grew up. And also uh, also Pop Foster, George Foster. That's another one, I always admired his bass playing. I always wished to play bass like him. And then uh, when I started playing bass, Liv Newton started me off and then I got hooked up with Chester, Chester Zardes. And I know the music some, but I didn't know very much. And Chester showed me how to uh, to swing. He showed me the swing part in the deal. Chester's the one who started me out. And uh, the voice uh, uh, Richard McClain liked me to music too. He taught me too. And also Pinchback Turo taught me. And uh, I had uh, Chester he showed me the swing in the band, how to play, learned me how to play.
In those days were you using the bow or picking?

I did more bowing than picking. Very little picking I did at that time. The uh, just on, on, on the, on the uh, beginning you'd, you'd, you'd start the bowing and maybe come out on the end you would pick a little bit.
The last chorus.
Yeah, the last chorus you might pick some. So I could bow better than I could pick at that time. But now I can pick better.
Did most of the bass players uh, pick or bow in those days?
Bow, bow. Most all of them. All of them bowed. Very few. Um, not very much picking.
And you remember the first one you heard pick? Did Newton pick too?
Yeah, he picked but he did more bowing. Mm-hmm. This guy Ellick was a very good picker and also a bow. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Do you remember Jimmy Johnson, the bass player?
Jimmy Johnson, yes, I remember him. I remember Jimmy Johnson. Bob Lyons. Who? Bob Lyons. Yeah, yeah, uh-huh.
Do you remember when you heard him? Who was he with there?

Oh, well I don't know, I can't recall who he was playing with at the time, cause I was kind of young you know, and I used to go around. When I used to go to these places I went with Liv, Liv Newton. You know, he carried me around everywhere he played, that's how I come to start the playing bass. And then I got away from it and I didn't play anymore for oh good while after, I may say about twelve, fifteen years. Later on then I picked up the bass again and I started the playing. So now.
What was the first band you played with?

The first band I ever got in with was Kid Rene. Kid Rene. Kid Rene come to my house and told me, asked me didn't I want to play with him. And I told him I didn't know if I could play good enough. He said, oh yes, I know you can play good enough. He said, sure. I said, I heard you playing around. He said, you play swell. He said, you come on. He said, you'll never get no place if you don't get in the band and go head on and play. Now that's the words he told me. So I said, well alright then. I said, I hope I don't mess the band up. I said, I hope I don't make a mess. So he said, okay. Well, you come on. You're going to do alright. So I went there and I mean everything was alright. So I was playing since.
Who else was in that band, do you remember?
Well, he had his brothers, Joe, playing drum. And let's see, who else was playing now?
It was the clarinet.
The clarinet. Let's see, who was that clarinet? Yes, I can't recall who he was. It's been so long.
It wasn't George Lewis then.
No, it wasn't George. It wasn't George at that time. It wasn't George because I could remember George. But it wasn't George. It was...
Do you remember clarinet's the name of George Boyd? George Boyd.
George Boyd. Oh, George Boyd. Yeah, yeah.
Was he playing with Rene at that time or somebody else?

He did play with Rene, but I don't think he played with it the time that I played with him. I don't think it was him. You could call somebody that I could recall back to, I could maybe, could say it was, I would know it.
You'll think of it later probably. Do you remember the trombone?

The trombone, let's see, who was the trombone? The trombone, it was, let's see, oh I think it was Jim, Jim Robison I think. Oh Jim? Yeah, I think it was Jim Robison playing the trombone. Yeah, I'm most sure it was Jim playing trombone.
Well that's most of them there except guitar, you remember a guitar player.
Yeah.
Or banjo.
Yeah, let's see, banjo, no, who was playing banjo, banjo? It wasn't as, let's see, should have had all that, that's all right. That's all right. That's didn't it. Of course.
Where did you play?
Well we played at some place up there, I think it was the, it's called St. Elizabeth Hall. Yeah, St. Elizabeth Hall, I think that was on Camp Street, Camp Valance. Uptown.
Yeah, mm-hmm.
That was the first job I played.
You played like weekend or Saturday night dances all the time?
Yeah, we played there I think three nights, three nights a week, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. Yeah.
Any other places ever played like out of Millenburg or Picnic?
Yes, I played a lot. I played Millenburg, I played Happy Landing, I played there for years, Happy Landing.
Who did you work there with?

Well I worked there with Georgie Parker, Happy Landing. I worked there about four or five years straight. Who else was in the band? Yeah, they had, let's see, Elmer Talbot was on trumpet and what you call him was on banjo was, well we call him Father Calley. He played, he played Father Calley. Father Calley, he played Father Calley we called him. He played guitar. And let's see, who was on the trombone, we have a trombone, yeah we have a trombone. Let's see who that was.
Well that's alright, do you remember any of the brass bands and trades when you were a kid?
Yeah, I remember quite a few of them. It's like Joe, I mean the tuba player.
Oh, Jackson.

Jackson, yeah. Data Jackson. Data Jackson, yeah. He used to play bass fiddle too. At the time when I started playing, trying to play bass. He was playing string bass then, he wouldn't play in tuba. Is that right? Oh sure, he started playing tuba after, way after that. I didn't know. He did, yeah.
Where did he come from? Aljaze, Aljaze.

Yeah, he came from Aljaze he did. Yeah, he played bass fiddle. And then he got on that tuba way late after, maybe he might have, he fooled with bass there a good while, because I remember I was a kid, I couldn't play then, I was too young. But he was playing bass fiddle then, along with Liv Newton then. And then also, let's see how I recall his name, boy, oh I know all them old timers. Let's see here. Well.
Well did you hear Kimball on the bass?
Kimball, yeah, sure. Henry Kimball was it? Henry Kimball, that's right, yes I heard Kimball on bass.
Do you remember where you heard him?

Well he played, he played, I can't recall exactly, Henry Kimball. Well I thought he played with, he played with, what you call him, some, Bebe Risley. Oh yeah. He played some with Bebe, I saw him, you know, when I was a kid play with Bebe.
Do you remember Bebe Risley?
Sure, I should say.
He's still there, right?
Oh yeah, yeah, he's paralyzed but he's still living, he's paralyzed, been paralyzed now for quite some time. Mm-hmm.
Well when did you leave New Orleans? How long have you been in California?
I've been in California, I left New Orleans in 1941.
Mm-hmm, 1941.
I left New Orleans first.
I left New Orleans in 1936. And I stayed out here a while and I went back and I come back in 41 and I stayed. First time I came in, in 36. Then I come back in, and 41 and I stayed then.
Tell me some more about the parade, the brass bands uptown. Were they big organized bands or just little pick up groups?

Well, most, you see like Bebe Risley, he had an organized band and also Kid O'Re had an organized band. On the street through the march, you know, you mean? Yeah, well they paraded too, like you know on advertising and parade around. Yeah, they did all of that also. And Jack Carey, he had an organized band. That's a good trombone man. Mm-hmm.
Don't have any pieces that they use. And those.
He used to use seven pieces with the piano. Out on the street? On the street six, not less than six. You mean on an advertised or a parade?
The brass band.

Oh, the brass band. Oh, twelve, fourteen, sixteen pieces like that. Oh yes, oh yes, oh yes. Twelve, fifteen, sixteen pieces. But I thought you meant on the advertised on the float like we advertise around. Yeah. Yeah, I played quite a few of them.
We'll talk about them later too. I was wondering more about those brass bands.
Yeah.
Did they all have uniforms in those days?
Yes, you see the brass band, you always had to have a uniform, you know, to show the parade. Quite natural, yes.
Usually wear coats though too? Now they don't wear coats anymore.
Well they had coats then. You had on the whole blue suit, you know, the whole blue suit, sure. Mm-hmm, those days.
And now all they wear is a cap and their dark pants and a white shirt.
Oh yeah, yeah, that's right now.
Remember about which instruments they had in the brass band?

Well they had... How many of each? How many? Well, on trumpet, they'd always have round about three trumpets. And on the trombone, two or three trombones. On the clarinets, two or three of those. Two or three of each, you know, brass.
Did they ever use saxophones in those days?
Sometime, yeah, sometime. Mm-hmm, yeah, the alto. Sometime. And mostly only one tuba though. Yeah. One tuba man and one kill drum. Bass drum. Bass drum.
Mm-hmm. On the wagons, did you ever play on the wagons?
Yeah, I played on the wagons several times. Yeah. We used to have a lot of fun playing on the advertising wagons.
How big a wagon was that? Was it a great big thing like a truck or were they fairly crowded when you got on?

It would be crowded because we hardly ever had the chances to get a big enough thing, you know, and they'd have six of us on there and most of the musicians sitting up in the front, they'd have to all be sitting down, you see, because sometime we'd play while the truck, mostly a mule pulling it. Yeah. Yeah, a horse or mule pulling that thing at that time, you know, a horse or a mule. Later on while we started with a truck, but on this beginning I'm talking about way back there, they had the mule or horse, one of the two was pulling, sometimes two, you know, two horses or two mules would be pulling this wagon, the big wagon, and we'd be piling, playing the bass man and the drum player would always be on the tailgate on the back, on the back playing the tailgate part, see.
You had the whole drum set, snare drum and bass and all?
Yeah, he had the whole deal up there, oh yeah, he had the whole deal up there. Where would the bass be?
Bass on the tailgate.
He's mostly on the tailgate. When he gets ready to knock off, he stands up on the tailgate, you see, and he plays right on the, he's peg on the tailgate.
Peg right out on the tailgate. Where would the trombone be?
The trombone, he's right next to the, right next to the back of the bass man, right by him, you know, up in front of him, but right in the back of him.
The trombone didn't always sit on the tailgate when he was on the tailgate?
Yeah, that's right, yeah, yeah, he did, right on the tailgate. He mostly, he mostly played, you know, out from the tailgate, the trombone man. That's right, yeah, yeah.
Then the clarinet and the clarinet were up in front of him.
That's right, they'd be up in the front, yeah.
Did anybody sit up in the driver's seat or you all sat in back? None of the musicians sat in back?
No, no, no, the musicians couldn't sit in the driver's seat, he had to stay on the, in the truck.
I thought there might be room for two up there if it was close by.
Yeah, but how could he play? He had to play. He couldn't play his instrument if he sat in the front. No. He'd have to sit, uh.
When he rode around, I thought maybe he'd sit up there sometime.
No, no, he'd always stayed there until we'd go around and end the load and then we'd all get off. That's the way, yeah.
You remember any, uh, what they call battles of music sometime when you'd run into another? Oh yeah, yeah, yeah.

You'd call that bucking. Bucking. Yeah, yeah, you'd call that bucking. We'd run, there's Kid Oren them, oh, Kid Oren and Jack Carey used to buck all the time. They was known for that, those two, you know. They really used to pick on each other. Both played trombone, you know, and they both had their own band. And they always, one would try to outdo the other one. That was, uh, that was Jack Carey and Kid Oren. When you hear that they was going to advertise Jack Carey and Kid Oren, boy that was a lot of fun there. And everybody was in the streets running behind those wagons to see that, see that bucking. Kid Oren and, uh, and, uh, and Jack Carey. Kid Oren and Jack Carey today is going to play. Kid Oren would, uh, when they'd see if they'd meet them, go around and listen for them. And they'd hear them, you know, and then they'd make their round and go right and meet each other, you know. And then they would stop on the corner. And they'd play a number. And then Jack Carey, he'd play a number. And then Oren, he'd play another number. That's right. See, see, they'd give him a dance, you know, and they was trying to, you know, swing the people to come to hear the real stuff and one was trying to outdo the other one, you know, and both of them was good. You just didn't know what was what. Because both was very good. Yeah.
Um, how much did they get paid for those jobs on the street?

Is that, oh my God, you want me to say this? Well, I tell you, at that time I have, uh, got no more than, uh, for advertising. Sometime you got a dollar and a quarter. Sometime you got a dollar. For the advertising.
And that was always, usually to advertise a dance, was it?

Yeah, that was for the dance for that night. For that night. Yeah. And you got a dollar, sometime you got a dollar, sometime you got a dollar and a quarter. How long would you be out on the street? Now the dance would play, where you're playing at would pay you a dollar and a quarter. You see? So then you made about two and a half there, you know, on that deal. So that was a pretty good deal at that time. Yeah, that was pretty good at that time. Yeah, that was good.
Yeah. Can you think of any other bands you played with? At different times back in the old days? In the old days.
Well, I played with, uh, I played with, uh...
After Kid Renee, after you left Kid Renee. Well, I played with Celestan, Papa.
I played with Papa Celestan quite a bit. And, uh, and I played with, uh, with, uh, I played with Kid Howard too.
Uh-huh.

And, uh, I'll tell you, I played with most all of them. I played some with all of them. That's right. I played some with all of them. I'll tell you the real fact. Yeah, I played some with all of them. Yeah, I know them all.
Um, just to put you on the spot now, who was the best bass player, either one or two best bass players you ever heard in your life? Ever heard in my life? I'll tell you.
Yeah, I'll tell you.
I'll tell you. Yeah, I'll tell you. You tried to copy after, you might say, model you're playing after.
Well, I'm gonna tell you. That is the truth. This is Chester. Chester's artist.
Chester's artist.

That's right. He's about the, he's about the, I would say, about the hardest working boy that I saw play bass. He's just about the hardest worker. I wouldn't say he the best, but that's the one I prefer. That's the one you like. And I play his own order, him, because he showed me the swing. Yeah. He showed me the swing. I had lots of other teachers and things, but he showed me the swing, he did. Yeah. Now, Lev Newton, he was kind of a, he liked it, he didn't like too much of, you know, too much of swinging too much, you know. He was a fine bass man, but he believed in, you know, not too much of swinging. But he's the one started me first.
Yeah.
And Chester's the one learned me how to swing. Yeah. And I play on the order. Everybody hear me play, say. So you play like Chester. Chester.
Even. Can you pick the bass, do you try to snap it onto the fingerboard or slap it any time? Sometime I do.

Sometime. Sometime I do. Sometime. Yeah. Sometime I'll slap it and then sometime I just pick it. Pick it, natural pick. Pull the strings while you get just nothing but tone. And sometime I'll slap. Mm-hmm.
I notice you use aluminum strings too, is it? On the. Yeah, I use the steel. Yeah. Two gut strings, aren't they?
Yeah, steel strings there. Yeah. And two guts.
Yeah, the lower two are wound.
Yeah, yeah. Yeah, steel. Steel. That's steel.
Yeah, you look good and have a nice bass.
Mm-hmm. Oh yeah. Yeah, that's a real good bass. I always kept a couple of basses and I prefer German bass. Mm-hmm. Yeah.
If you had to make a choice in picking a trumpet player or a cornet, who would be your favorite on that if you ever heard?
You mean back time, years ago?
Any time, yeah.
Oh, any time or years ago?
Well, years ago too.

Well, I got, see I got, today I like Mike on trumpet, Mike DeLay. Yeah, he is very good. I like Mike DeLay on trumpet very much. And now back further, I think the kid was great. Kid Renee. Kid Renee, yeah, I think he was great. And another boy is very good too. He's nice, he had a kind of stroke now, but he's always, he was always, well with me, I mean for his playing is concerned, it was Kid Howard. Oh, Kid Howard. And another guy I like, he was kind of weak, but I liked him too. It was Elmer Talbot called Cuckoo. He's a good one too. But he was a little weak cause he had had a slight stroke. Yeah. But he's pretty good.
How did Kid Renee play? Did he play low or high or?
At times, yeah, at times. He played low, sometimes high.
Did he have a big powerful tone? Was he?
Very, very strong. Very strong. He had lots of chops. Yeah, he had good chops. Very good chops. Kid had very good chops.
Who was the best drummer you can remember working with or hearing in the old days?
Working with?
I think you heard when you were a kid even if you can remember.

Well, I think I would pick, I'll pick Nene out of all of them. I'll pick Nene way back there. He was a wonderful drummer. Yeah, he was a good drummer. Yeah, for jazz. Very good. Had the right beat. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. You really could swing, you know, with them hitting the drums.
What about clarinet players? Who were the best in those days?

Well, the clarinet player? Well, I think, let's see, well, let's see who I got on clarinet there I used to like so much was, well, I would say George. George is the man I always liked on clarinet. George Lewis. George Lewis. Yeah. I liked the George on.
Do you remember any of the men before him like T.O. or Bach K?
Well, T.O. or Bach K, well I just know of them. Johnny Dodds. Johnny Dodds of him. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He left a good while ago. I remember about him though.
Do you remember Georgia Boy? Georgia Boy, yeah.
What did he play? Well, that was, he played, Georgia Boy played, what you call him, didn't he? Georgia Boy.
The clarinetist, I mean.

Yeah, that's what I say. He played the clarinet too. Georgia Boy. That was another good one. You made me think of that. Yeah, I remember him, yeah. Yeah, Georgia Boy was very good on clarinet. Do you remember Zeb?
Zeb, yeah.
Well, see Zeb. I remember that, I remember that name. I remember that name Zeb though. Yeah.
You might tell some of the other halls where you used to play or where you heard music when you were young.
Yeah, well, uh, see like.
There's places where they gave dances up town.
Yeah, Miss Coles. Oh yeah, what kind of, what were they?
Lawn parties, huh? Yeah, that's right.

Well it was a dance hall, you know, that first was lawn parties, years ago, and then she made a dance hall. She did? Yeah, regular big dance hall. Did she build it out in their yard? Build it, build it in that big vacant place where we used to have the, she used to have the lawn parties. Where was that? That was on, on, let's see, on Woola. On Woola and, Woola and Jackson, Jackson Woola. I don't think it was, Jackson Clare or Jackson Woola? Josephine somebody told me it was. Josephine, well between Josephine and Jackson. Well, Willa and Josephine. Willa and Josephine, well that's right, well Jackson the next year, yeah, yeah. So she built a dance hall in there. Yeah, she built a dance hall there. We used to go there when we were just little kids, you know, to lawn parties.
Did they have them every week or night or when?

Yeah, every weekend. No, every weekend. Every weekend. And then, of course the, uh, Miss, uh, let's see, Miss Coles and then also, uh, the, uh, St. Elizabeth Hall. That was on camp in Valens. And then, come the, uh, the, uh, let's see, St. Dominic Hall. St. Dominic Hall. What street that was on again? I forgot.
I want to hear a little bit more about the, Miss Coles. Miss Coles? Did they charge you?
Oh yes, you had to pay fifteen cents. Did they have drinks or anything to eat? Nothing hard to drink, just soft drinks and sandwiches and things like that. You bought that then? Yeah, that's right.
How long were those? But those last three or later they quit pretty early.
No, they quit around three o'clock. Start around eight until about three.
Well, there's only another minute or so left. Is there anything else you'd like to tell about your life that you can think of? Well... Or your playing, your music, anything at all?
Well, I think a lot of playing and music, you know, I really like music. I'm a builder. My father was a builder. Yes, you do. And then I stepped in on that, you know, from a kid too.
You say some of these men helped you to read, so you learned to read music then too?

Yes, yes. Well, the first one really learned me how to... I had been, you know, spelling a little bit and Richard McClane, he started me reading. And then I got with Pinchback and he showed me the rest. And then I goes on to this guy, Wilcox, and he showed me some about reading, so that's how I learned how to read. Did you ever find that big WPA band they had during the... No, I, no, no, I couldn't get on the WPA. They wouldn't ever put me on. No. No, they wouldn't put me in that band. And a lot of musicians. Yeah, they had a lot of them, but you had to, you had to pull some straws to get in that thing. Yeah. Yeah, you could, I couldn't get in it.
Your wife came from downtown, you're saying you moved downtown later.
No, no, my wife came, we came from around the same place. Yeah. See, I got married when I was 16. Oh, that early. Yeah, I got married when I was 16. She was 15, I was 16.
